title: RISC-V as a Research Platform
excerpt: Why an open instruction set becomes much more interesting when the goal is not just to run programs, but to make architectural behaviour measurable, reproducible, and experimentally useful.

body.text: Why RISC-V Is Interesting

RISC-V is interesting to me for a reason that goes beyond the instruction set itself. Its open ISA makes it a useful platform for asking questions about computer architecture, operating systems, compilers, and performance without treating the processor as a completely opaque object.
From Programs to Machine Behaviour

When working close to the machine, a small C or assembly program becomes an experiment. Instructions are fetched, decoded, executed, and reflected in architectural state. Following that path forces connections between abstractions that are often taught separately.
Controlled Workloads

This is one reason I have been exploring RISC-V alongside operating systems and computer architecture. Writing small programs is one layer. Running them on a RISC-V environment is another. Studying their behaviour through simulation and traces adds another layer where architectural questions become measurable.
RISC-V as a Laboratory

The interesting part is the boundary between software and the machine. A workload has a structure: branches, memory accesses, arithmetic operations, dependencies, and instruction mixes. A processor responds to that structure through pipelines, caches, prediction, queues, and execution resources.
The Larger Lesson

That perspective is central to my LowBIt work. I am interested in small, deterministic programs that can act as controlled experiments rather than opaque benchmark binaries. If the workload is reproducible, architectural measurements can be compared more carefully across configurations.

title: What gem5 Actually Teaches About Computer Architecture
excerpt: Simulation makes processor behaviour visible, but looking closely at CPU models, memory systems, and execution reveals why architectural experiments need careful experimental design.

body.text: From Diagrams to Experiments
A computer architecture diagram can make a processor look wonderfully tidy. Fetch, decode, execute, memory, and writeback fit into a few boxes. A detailed simulator quickly removes that simplicity.
Out-of-Order Execution

Working with gem5 has been one way for me to move from architecture diagrams toward experiments. Instead of only asking how a processor should behave, I can ask what happens when a particular workload is executed under a particular CPU and memory configuration.
Experimental Validity

This becomes especially interesting with out-of-order execution. Instructions do not necessarily complete in the same order in which the program presents them. Dependencies, speculation, queues, execution resources, and memory behaviour all influence forward progress.
Debugging as an Architecture Lesson

The simulator also teaches an important distinction between architectural correctness and experimental usefulness. A configuration can be technically valid while still being a poor instrument for the question being asked. The CPU model, workload, cache configuration, simulation mode, and measurement method all matter.
gem5 as an Experimental Instrument

Debugging a simulation can therefore become an architecture lesson. A stalled instruction stream, an unexpected memory access, or a run that fails to make forward progress can reveal interactions between the workload, the simulated machine, and the simulator configuration.

title: Learning Through Derivatives
excerpt: A mathematical view of neural-network learning, where derivatives turn parameter changes into a measurable path from error to update.

body.text: The Derivative Behind Learning

The phrase 'the neural network learns' can make learning sound almost magical. Underneath the terminology is a repeated numerical process: measure an error, determine how the error changes with respect to the parameters, and update those parameters.
Seeing Gradient Descent

The derivative is the key piece. If changing a parameter slightly increases the loss, the gradient indicates that the parameter should move in the opposite direction. The update is therefore guided by local information about the loss function.
Backpropagation Through Layers

I find this easier to understand visually than through equations alone. Plotting the loss as a function of a parameter turns gradient descent into movement across a mathematical landscape. The network is not searching randomly for an answer. It is following information encoded in the gradient.
Building Intuition with Small Networks

Backpropagation extends this idea through multiple layers. The chain rule lets us determine how a change in one parameter affects the final loss through all the intermediate operations between that parameter and the output.
A General Mathematical View

Building small neural networks makes the distinction between forward propagation and learning much clearer. Forward propagation produces a prediction. Backpropagation computes how the parameters contributed to the error. The optimizer then uses that information to change the parameters.

title: When Direction Matters More Than Magnitude
excerpt: An experiment with magnitude-direction representations that asks whether separating a vector's scale from its geometry can reveal structure hidden by ordinary representations.

body.text: Separating Magnitude and Direction
Most machine-learning pipelines treat a feature vector as one object. But a non-zero vector contains at least two distinct pieces of information: its magnitude and its direction.
What MNIST Revealed

For a non-zero vector x, we can write x = r u, where r = ||x|| is the magnitude and u = x / ||x|| is the normalized direction. This simple decomposition creates an interesting question: what happens if a model is asked to learn from these components separately?
Beyond Concatenation

In my MNIST experiments, magnitude alone was weak for the classification task, while direction carried substantially more information. Combining magnitude and direction provided additional information, but the result also suggested that the interaction between the two components deserved closer study.
Geometry and Dimensionality Reduction

That led to a broader question. Perhaps the important issue is not simply whether magnitude and direction are useful, but whether magnitude should influence how directional information is represented. Instead of merely concatenating the two, one can explore magnitude-conditioned transformations of the directional representation.
The Broader Question

This line of experimentation became part of my exploration of spherical representations and the Spherical Representation Transformation Neuron framework. The useful question is not whether a single representation wins on one dataset. It is whether there are classes of data for which the geometry of a representation provides a better inductive structure.

title: Building a LowBIt Trace Corpus
excerpt: A research direction connecting deterministic programs, execution traces, RISC-V, and computer architecture to build a reusable foundation for workload and performance analysis.

body.text: Why Build a Trace Corpus
Benchmarks are useful because they turn vague claims about performance into measurable experiments. But a benchmark is only as interesting as the questions it allows us to ask.
Controlled Workloads

My current LowBIt direction is to build a trace corpus around carefully designed workloads and low-bit computation. The goal is not simply to collect execution logs, but to create a structured dataset connecting programs with measurable execution and architectural behaviour.
The LowBIt Benchmark Direction

The basic idea is to run a diverse collection of small programs, collect relevant execution information, and organize the resulting traces so that they can be reused for analysis and benchmarking. A large collection of controlled workloads can expose patterns that a handful of hand-picked examples cannot.
A RISC-V-First Extension

The benchmark side of LowBIt focuses on lightweight and deterministic workloads. The current ecosystem includes LB-ML-001, a transformer scaled dot-product attention kernel designed around reproducible workloads and reference validation.
What Makes a Corpus Useful

A broader RISC-V-first research direction extends this idea toward branch-prediction and cache-behaviour characterization. The intended taxonomy uses combinations of controlled branch and cache patterns to produce many small deterministic C programs.
Research Infrastructure

The value of the corpus is therefore not just its size. Its usefulness depends on reproducibility, metadata, clear workload definitions, consistent metrics, and a generation pipeline that makes experiments repeatable.

title: Looking at Operating-System Synchronization Through Symmetry
excerpt: An attempt to describe synchronization and scheduling using permutation groups, turning familiar operating-system mechanisms into questions about symmetry and restrictions.

body.text: A Different View of Synchronization

Operating-system synchronization is usually introduced through locks, semaphores, monitors, critical sections, and scheduling policies. I became interested in a different description: what if some of these behaviours could be understood through symmetry?
Processes and Permutations

A collection of processes can be viewed as objects that may be permuted. The symmetric group S_n provides a natural mathematical language for describing these permutations and the restrictions imposed by synchronization.
Synchronization as Restriction

From this perspective, a synchronization rule can be interpreted as restricting which transformations of the process configuration are allowed. Mutual exclusion, for example, can be related to stabilizing a configuration in which a critical resource cannot be simultaneously occupied by multiple processes.
Scheduling as Transformation

Scheduling adds another layer. A schedule is not merely a list of processes. It is a transformation of which process is allowed to make progress at each point. Cyclic actions provide a natural mathematical picture for round-robin-style behaviour.
Why the Algebra Matters

The interesting part is not replacing operating-system terminology with abstract algebra for its own sake. The goal is to ask whether the algebra exposes structure that is difficult to see in the usual implementation-level description.
Toward a Mathematical Model

My work on this direction includes formalization in S_n and the definition and refinement of a metric structure intended for geometric analysis. The remaining questions concern how to interpret the resulting metric structure and how the computational model should be tuned.

This project sits at an intersection I particularly enjoy: operating systems on one side, abstract algebra and mathematical structure on the other. The computer system becomes a place where an abstract mathematical object can acquire operational meaning.
